generatedProse.concept-context: Getting the most out of a practice experience is a matter of initiative across three phases. Before you start, prepare: set your aims, read up on the setting, and agree with your supervisor how they can help. While you are there, engage: volunteer for real tasks, ask why something is done a certain way, watch how experienced people work, and seek feedback early. Afterwards, consolidate: record what you did and learned, and connect it to your development and your plans.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students spending a term on the same project placement.

Student A waits to be given jobs and does them well enough. When an instruction is unclear, Student A guesses rather than asks, and never requests feedback for fear of seeming unsure. The work passes, but no one stretches it, and the placement ends much as it began.

Student B asks, on the first day, what would make the term useful to the team, and volunteers for work just beyond their current skill. When something is unclear, Student B checks early; after each task, they ask what could be stronger. By the end, Student B has done harder work, learned faster, and is remembered when a reference is needed.

Same project, same length. Student B took the initiative that turned time into learning.
generatedProse.summary: You get the most out of a practice experience by being proactive across three phases: preparing and aiming before, taking initiative and seeking feedback during, and recording and connecting afterwards. You can now apply these strategies, tell a proactive approach from a passive one, and choose an active move when you are in the thick of it. The last lesson is about showing what all this produced: how practice is assessed, and how to evidence your learning.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Student B's term more productive than Student A's?

items.text: Student B took the initiative: asking, volunteering for stretch, and seeking feedback early.
Student B was given easier tasks that were simpler to complete.
Student B avoided asking questions so as not to seem unsure.
Student B waited to be told exactly what to do at each step.

feedback.correct: That's right. Student B took the initiative, asking, volunteering and seeking feedback, which turned the term into learning.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Student B did rather than waited for.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Student B's term was more productive because of initiative: asking, volunteering for stretch and seeking feedback early, rather than waiting, playing safe or guessing.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; name the cast directly in the prose (the pack supplies the whole body). The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
